There are a couple of different ways to completely disconnect yourself from the grid once the solar system is installed.

  1. All circuits powered by solar should be moved from your main breaker to a new breaker panel and then through a single breaker in the main panel). Switching the single breaker in the main panel disconnects the grid from the circuits getting solar since they get power from both the grid AND solar)

  2. You equipment should also have a "box" with a couple of different switches inside. In mine, I have a main switch which switches off the solar but there's a switch inside which allows me to disconnect it from the grid and run entirely on solar.

  3. The local power company required a switch-box outside to allow me to completely disconnect from the grid.

So I have two ways to disconnect my solar powered circuits from the grid as well as the outside switch to disconnect from the grid completely.

If you have a battery backup system, there's a box inside your house that switches you from grid to just solar when the grid power goes down.

Tax credits are subtracted not from taxable income, but directly from a person’s tax liability; they therefore reduce taxes dollar for dollar. As a result, credits have the same value for everyone who can claim their full value.

So... you can get up to 30% of the cost of the system back. If you own a house, car, property, pay enough taxes, that helps because you can claim those as reductions. Your amount of taxes paid becomes $0 up to the amount of the solar system. However, if the amount of taxes you were supposed to pay is... let's say $5000, and you paid every bit of that, you get $5000 back but not the total of $10,000 (assuming your system costs $30K.)

So for me, I have a really good paying job which gives me a tax liability of $12,651 (meaning I'm supposed to pay that much in taxes before credits and deductions). I do that very easily. I also get tax credits/deductions for house and property tax, car tax, student loan interest taxes and a few other things. So this year, I actually get about a paycheck's worth of refund and will do so next year because I actually overpay (by choice). Add to the fact that I'm still paying my liability of about $12K and that means that I'm good for a LOT of cash back at tax time.
